speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: The Auditor-General (AG) is empowered to audit public entities or bodies that administer public funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: The AG conducts independent audits of Government finances, checks for financial irregularities and ascertains whether there has been excess, extravagance or gross inefficiency in the use of public funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: These audits give assurance to the President and Parliament on the proper accounting, management and use of public resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: However, the work of the Government has expanded and become more complex over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: The Government is increasingly involving a wide range of non-government entities in public service delivery, such as restructured hospitals, autonomous universities, voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), charities, preschool operators, Town Councils and outsourced contractors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: Substantial public funds are also disbursed to non-government entities for various purposes, such as for economic or social development for the benefit of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: Collectively, this amounts to several billions of dollars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: Hence, there is a need to enhance the audit powers of the AG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: This is not unique, as other countries around the world see the same trend in terms of involving more non-government entities to deliver public services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: Jurisdictions, including Canada, the United Kingdom (UK), Australia, Denmark, Sweden and Finland all empower their national auditors to conduct "follow-the-dollar" audits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: The audits will not extend to non-government entities' use of their own funds or funds from other sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: I wish to emphasise that it is not the intention in this Bill for the AG to take over the role of private sector auditors who will continue to audit these non-government entities as they are now doing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: This is a similar approach to a range of other local statutes, where the Minister responsible for the subject matter – in this case, public finances – has the power to direct that certain things be done in order to protect the public interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: An example would be when, let us say, a VWO has been appointed by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) to disburse public funds to the needy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: However, there are reasons to suspect that the VWO has used the funds for staff benefits instead of channelling them to the needy as intended.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: Or take another example: an autonomous university (AU) is given a sum of money by the Ministry of Education (MOE) which is meant to be disbursed as education bursaries for students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: However, there may be reasons to believe, whether from MOE's ordinary checks or otherwise, that the money is being used for other purposes instead, such as the recruitment of academic staff or for the purchase of research equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: In these cases, the Minister for Finance can direct that a "follow-the-dollar" audit be conducted on the VWO or the university.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: The AG will be empowered to audit whether the public funds given to the VWO or the university have been used according to the terms and conditions set out by MSF and MOE respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: In short, "follow-the-dollar" audits will apply to recipients of public funds, and only undertaken in cases where it is in the public interest to do so, and the audit will only be limited to whether the funding terms and conditions have been complied with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: In order for a "follow-the-dollar" audit to be conducted, the AG will need to have the necessary powers to discharge his duty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: In line with the powers granted to the National Audit Organisations in other jurisdictions, such as Australia and New Zealand, the AG and his authorised representatives will be empowered to enter and remain in any premises occupied by the subject of the audit, or premises occupied by someone who holds custody of the required information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: AGO will also be able to search for and inspect documents, information and records.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: Such powers are already given to officers of the Energy Market Authority (EMA) or the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) when they need to perform enforcement functions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: To conclude, the amendments to the Audit Act will provide powers to the AG to conduct "follow-the-dollar" audits on non-government entities' use of public funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: This is to ensure that public funds are used for the purposes for which they are intended and to enable accountability of public spending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: The amendments keep the powers of the AG updated and relevant in an operating context where non-government entities are increasingly receiving public funds to help deliver a range of services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah) (on behalf of the Minister for Finance)
text: This will enable the AG to fulfil his role of strengthening financial governance and ensuring accountability for the use of public resources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides direct service by public agencies, increasingly, much of the public services and public goods are contracted out to private sectors and the not-for-profit sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government also disburses a substantial amount of public money in the form of grants and subsidies to a wide range of organisations, such as restructured hospitals, VWOs and the Town Councils, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, the Government also provides performance guarantees to help finance infrastructural projects and undertake utility payments in public-private partnership (PPP) projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Going forward, there will be more varied, more complex and more innovative arrangements where public money will go to non-government sectors, which could be multi-layered and multi-dimensional.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is unavoidable as the Government seeks to carry out its public functions and specific policy executions in the most efficient, most effective and optimal way, drawing on the strengths and expertise of the private and non-government sectors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, the Government also used its budgetary resources to subsidise services and programmes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the Government kept the costs of municipal services affordable by giving cash grants to Town Councils to help keep down the costs of estate maintenance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another example, the Ministry of Transport (MOT) also injects funds to the public transport operators (PTOs) to help reduce the capital costs of enhancing public transport, such as the Bus Service Enhancement Programme (BSEP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And there are increasingly more of such programmes as the Government intervenes to improve public services, to build economic and security capabilities or to increase its social spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would continue to be the modus operandi in the way the future whole-of-Government would work.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We know that as the delivery of services and its accounting on the use of funds are further away from the direct view of Government audit, the risk of improper or corrupt conduct would increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There may be instances where public money may need to be disbursed to non-government sectors or agencies to carry out emergency tasks, such as in a disaster recovery situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is hence appropriate to have some executive leeway.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) should also monitor the impact of these changes to private sector companies who are receiving public funding.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many countries have empowered their National Audit Offices to audit on the "follow-the-dollar" basis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Overall, I believe that it will reduce the possibility of improper conduct and strengthen trust in public finance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Enhancing the AG's powers to ensure public accountability of public monies is welcomed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is subject to a carve-out that any such explanation, information, document, record or answer provided cannot be used as evidence against an individual in civil or criminal proceedings and can only be used in proceedings under section 177 of the Penal Code or an offence relating to the falsity of the answer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Audit Act, as it currently stands, includes a broad obligation in section 6(3) where an individual called upon for any explanation or information is "legally bound to furnish such explanation and information".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On a literal plain reading, this suggests that section 177 of the Penal Code would already apply if this section 6(3) obligation was contravened by an individual, even without the amendments in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On a comparative note, another legislation, which confers such a broad obligation, is the Prevention of Corruption Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau officers have the power to require a person to "give any information on any subject" relating to corruption cases and the person so questioned is "legally bound to give that information".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the Prevention of Corruption Act, there is no specific provision excluding the common law privilege against self-incrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this context, given that such a broad obligation exists to compel an individual to furnish explanation and information, with the relevant penalty provision in section 177 of Penal Code already in place, can the Minister clarify the intent of specifically excluding this privilege against self-incrimination in this Bill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand from the Explanatory Notes that this new section 6A will help ensure the efficiency of the audit process is not diminished by the AG and his officers having to engage in time-consuming negotiations about the provision of privileged documents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the nature of inquiries by the AG does have potentially wide and severe implications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how this new section 6A will allow the AG to better carry out its primary work of ensuring public accountability of the Government to Parliament, in the event that an explanation, information, document, record or answer obtained under section 6A does, in fact, raise concerns which ought to, in public's interest, lead to civil or criminal prosecution?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa highlighted the need to ensure that we do not add to the regulatory burden of companies and that there should be some executive leeway given for situations where public money may be given to non-government entities to carry out emergency tasks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We agree that the right balance needs to be struck and will be mindful that the scope and the extent of the audit should be commensurate with the circumstances of the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amendments have been designed to avoid adding to the regulatory burden of companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The "follow-the-dollar" audits are not meant to replace the normal audit processes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I explained in my speech, "follow-the-dollar" audits will not be activated lightly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The threshold for triggering such audits is high.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It can only be directed by the Minister for Finance and only if he is satisfied that it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The audits will also only be limited to whether the funding terms and conditions have been complied with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the intent of specifically excluding the privilege against self-incrimination in this Bill, given that there exists a broad obligation to compel an individual to furnish explanation and information to the AG.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By stating this clearly, we can avoid time-consuming negotiations to clarify the obligations on the provision of privileged documents which will diminish the efficiency of the audit process.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is consistent with the drafting approach adopted for legislation in the recent years, for instance, in the recently passed amendments to the Town Councils Act, the Banking Act and the Securities and Futures Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked what would happen if information obtained from the individual under the claim of self-interest does raise concerns which ought to lead to civil or criminal prosecution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These agencies would have access to more extensive powers of investigation, which would then allow them to obtain the necessary evidence to proceed with the civil or criminal prosecution.
